source.contracts.py:
"""Small, dependency-free records exchanged by AnaxiGraph components.

The graph contains observations. Annotations and reviews carry their own basis,
evidence and source identity; they never silently become source facts.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Protocol


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Node:
    id: str
    kind: str
    name: str
    path: str
    line: int = 1
    data: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Edge:
    source: str
    target: str
    kind: str
    path: str
    line: int = 1
    resolution: str = "resolved"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Snapshot:
    id: str
    root: str
    revision: str | None
    dirty: bool
    files: dict[str, str]
    created_at: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Graph:
    snapshot: Snapshot
    nodes: tuple[Node, ...]
    edges: tuple[Edge, ...]
    diagnostics: tuple[str, ...] = ()

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return asdict(self)


class KnowledgeStore(Protocol):
    """The application owns workflow; the store owns atomic persistence."""

    def save_graph(self, graph: Graph) -> None: ...

    def load_graph(self, root: str, snapshot_id: str | None = None) -> Graph | None: ...

    def annotate(
        self,
        root: str,
        snapshot_id: str,
        node_id: str,
        annotation: dict[str, Any],
        *,
        expected_digest: str | None = None,
    ) -> None: ...

    def search(self, root: str, query: str, limit: int = 20) -> list[dict[str, Any]]: ...

    def save_review(
        self, root: str, snapshot_id: str, review_id: str, kind: str, result: dict[str, Any]
    ) -> None: ...

    def reviews(self, root: str, kind: str | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]: ...

    def stats(self, root: str) -> dict[str, Any]: ...

alternatives.name: Immutable domain records with a narrow storage port
alternatives.design: Define frozen Node, Edge, Snapshot, and Graph records as the shared domain vocabulary. Graph owns conversion of itself and nested records to dictionary data, using the dataclass data representation. Snapshot carries revision, dirty state, file identifiers, and creation time; observations carry source locations and resolution status. A storage protocol is a capability boundary for graph retrieval/persistence, annotation, search, review listing/handling, and statistics. It states that persistence is atomic by store responsibility without prescribing a mechanism. Retrieval permits no graph and an optional snapshot identifier. Annotation accepts an optional expected digest but leaves its checking semantics unstated. Search defaults to 20 and leaves matching, order, and unusual-limit behavior open; review listing accepts an optional kind filter and leaves further semantics open. State and conversion responsibility sit in domain records; consistency and atomicity behavior sit with each store implementation; callers own interpretation of unspecified semantics.
pros: Small conceptual surface with a direct mapping from requirements to records and protocol methods.
Frozen records make reassignment constraints visible at construction boundaries.
Keeps atomicity implementation-specific and avoids inventing consistency or search semantics.
cons: A broad storage protocol can couple clients to several capabilities even when they need only one.
The domain records carry most representational responsibility; adding validation or richer lifecycle rules later could make them crowded.
Unspecified semantics can lead independent stores to behave differently unless callers document their expectations.

alternatives.name: Snapshot package with explicit codec and repository boundary
alternatives.design: Treat a graph plus its repository snapshot metadata as a frozen SnapshotPackage, with frozen node, edge, and graph records nested within it. Observation records retain source location and resolution status; the package identifies revision, dirty state, file identifiers, and creation time. Put dictionary conversion in an explicit codec that recursively emits dataclass data representation, rather than on Graph itself. Define a repository-facing storage port for retrieval/persistence, annotation, search, review handling, and statistics. The port declares atomic persistence as a store guarantee, supports retrieval with no graph and optional snapshot ID, and accepts an optional expected digest for annotation without defining the comparison outcome. Search has default limit 20 with matching/order/unusual-limit behavior unspecified; review listing accepts optional kind with other semantics unspecified. The package owns immutable state grouping, codec owns representation, and adapters own storage behavior. This adds a boundary useful when serialized data and in-memory records have separate evolution needs.
pros: Separates persisted dictionary shape from domain record structure, which can help when formats evolve.
Makes the graph-to-snapshot association explicit as one package passed across boundaries.
Keeps storage guarantees and unspecified operation semantics at the adapter boundary.
cons: Adds a package and codec layer beyond the minimal record-plus-protocol design.
Callers must know or receive the codec to convert graphs, rather than invoking conversion directly on Graph.
A package wrapper can be cumbersome for operations that only need a graph or only need snapshot metadata.

alternatives.name: Use-case ports with capability-specific storage responsibilities
alternatives.design: Keep the required frozen Node, Edge, Snapshot, and Graph records, with observations carrying source location and resolution status and snapshots carrying revision, dirty state, file identifiers, and creation time. Graph conversion returns its recursive dataclass data representation as a dictionary. Instead of one all-purpose storage interface, describe a small storage capability set: graph access/persistence, annotation, search, review operations, and statistics, composed where a client needs multiple capabilities. The graph persistence capability declares atomicity as the implementation's responsibility without specifying its mechanism. Retrieval allows no graph and optional snapshot ID. Annotation accepts optional expected digest but does not promise a particular check. Search defaults to 20 and leaves matching/order/unusual-limit semantics open; review listing accepts optional kind and does not add unspecified ordering or filtering guarantees. This changes how interface obligations are delivered: clients depend on the operation groups they use, while implementations may compose them. Complexity is justified when consumers have distinct responsibilities; for a small single-client system the capability split is extra ceremony and the first design is simpler.
pros: Separates interface obligations by responsibility and can keep clients focused on needed operations.
Allows storage implementations to compose capabilities according to their supported duties.
Leaves all declared optional parameters and deliberately unspecified semantics intact.
cons: More interface types and composition decisions increase setup and navigation cost.
Atomic persistence responsibility must be clearly associated with graph persistence even when capabilities are composed.
For one consumer or one implementation, splitting the port may add complexity without reducing coupling.

data.docstring:
Small, dependency-free records exchanged by AnaxiGraph components.

The graph contains observations. Annotations and reviews carry their own basis,
evidence and source identity; they never silently become source facts.

capabilities: Represent graph observations as structured records with source locations and resolution status.
Associate graph data with a repository snapshot, including revision, dirty state, file identifiers, and creation time.
Convert a graph record and its nested records into dictionary data.
Describe a storage interface for graph retrieval and persistence, node annotation, search, review handling, and statistics.

contracts.statement: Node, edge, snapshot, and graph records are declared frozen, so their fields cannot be reassigned after construction.
The graph conversion operation returns the dataclass data representation as a dictionary.
The persistence interface describes atomic persistence as the store's responsibility; the protocol does not define how atomicity is achieved.
Graph retrieval may return no graph, and its snapshot identifier is optional.
Annotation accepts an optional expected digest, which by its name suggests a conditional consistency check; the protocol does not specify the check's behavior.
Search uses a default limit of 20, while the protocol does not define matching, ordering, or behavior for unusual limits.
Review listing accepts an optional kind filter; the protocol does not specify ordering or filtering semantics beyond that parameter.

annotation.detail: The records represent nodes and edges with source locations, snapshot identity and file state, and a graph that groups a snapshot with its nodes, edges, and diagnostics. Graph data can be converted to a nested dictionary. The persistence protocol describes operations for storing and retrieving graphs, attaching annotations, searching, recording and listing reviews, and obtaining statistics; its method declarations do not specify backend behavior.

functions.overview: Returns the graph and its nested record data as a dictionary.
Declares an operation to attach annotation data to a node in a selected snapshot, optionally guarded by an expected digest.
Declares retrieval of a graph for a repository root and optional snapshot identifier, with no graph represented by a nullable result.
Declares retrieval of review records for a repository root, optionally filtered by kind.
Declares storage of a graph.
Declares storage of a result under a review identifier and kind for a selected snapshot.
Declares search within a repository root with a query and default result limit of 20.
Declares retrieval of statistics for a repository root.

annotation.overview: This module defines immutable records for repository observations and a persistence interface for graphs, annotations, searches, reviews, and statistics.
uncertainty: The protocol declares method shapes but does not establish concrete persistence behavior, error handling, ordering, search semantics, or digest validation rules.
